posts.title: UK crypto activity fell 8% this year.
posts.author: WEB3 Newswire
posts.snippet:
UK crypto activity fell 8% this year. 
UK domestic stablecoin transfers grew nearly 20 times.

Both are true, and they’re in the same Chainalysis report.

Western Europe’s crypto economy came in at $2.08 trillion between July 2025 and June 2026, up 1.2%. 

Not much, but it’s one of only three regions that grew at all, alongside Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.

The UK is still the biggest market at $424.5 billion. 

It shrank 8%, mostly because decentralized exchange trading dropped off.

But look under that number. Domestic stablecoin transfers in the UK went from $109 million to $2.09 billion. 

That’s 60% of all domestic stablecoin transfer value in Western Europe, more than the rest of the region combined. 

Fewer people are trading. 
More people are moving money.

Across the region, stablecoin holdings in personal wallets rose 131%, against 52% globally. 

Western Europe’s share of global stablecoin balances went from 3.4% to 5.1%.

France tells its own story. 

Stablecoin balances in personal wallets rose 192%, and the number of French wallets holding them went from 3,577 to 12,255. 

Stablecoins now make up 54.2% of French withdrawals from centralized exchanges, the highest among the big markets.

The regulatory backdrop is moving fast too. The EBA just named Circle’s USDC the first significant e-money token under MiCA. 

The Dutch bank consortium Qivalis has its license, though its euro stablecoin isn’t in circulation yet. 

In the UK, the FCA application window runs until the end of February, ahead of the new regime in October 2027.

The pattern worth sitting with: speculation is cooling, utility isn’t.

#Stablecoins #Chainalysis #Europe #UK #MiCA #Web3 #DigitalAssets
posts.reason: Substantive analysis of European stablecoin adoption, MiCA implementation and regulatory regime changes directly engages their core CASP/token practice and target audience.

comments.text: The stablecoin growth masks a regulatory distinction worth flagging: holding or transferring an e-money token under MiCAR is not the same as providing a CASP service, and plenty of firms riding this growth are about to find they need authorisation for activity they thought was just custody or payments infrastructure.

With the FCA window closing in February ahead of the October 2027 regime, how many of the UK firms currently driving that stablecoin volume do you think are actually scoping whether they'll need authorisation versus assuming they fall outside it?

We're seeing the same pattern on the continent - clients are far more worried about CASP authorisation and the VASP transition deadline than about token price action, which tracks with your point that utility is what's actually moving.

posts.title: Coffeezilla and researcher Molly White just published a long investigation into the Trump family’s crypto businesses.
posts.author: WEB3 Newswire
posts.snippet:
Coffeezilla and researcher Molly White just published a long investigation into the Trump family’s crypto businesses.

The headline item isn’t theirs. 

It comes from The Wall Street Journal, which reported that an Abu Dhabi vehicle backed by Sheikh Tahnoon, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49% of World Liberty Financial for $500 million. 

The deal was signed four days before the January 2025 inauguration, by Eric Trump. 

According to the WSJ, half was paid upfront, and $187 million of that went to Trump family entities.

World Liberty confirmed the investment and says neither Trump nor Steve Witkoff was involved. 

Trump has said he was unaware of it and that his sons handle the business.

The investigation then follows a related thread. 

MGX, the Abu Dhabi firm Tahnoon chairs, used World Liberty’s USD1 stablecoin for its $2 billion investment in Binance. 

For a young stablecoin, that’s a large chunk of circulating supply, and stablecoin reserves earn income. 

World Liberty says MGX chose USD1 on its merits and that it has no influence over government policy.

Other threads in the report: 

Justin Sun’s $75 million investment while facing an SEC case that was later resolved, CZ’s pardon, and a Crypto.com partnership with Trump Media after the SEC closed its probe. 

White also says the TRUMP and MELANIA tokens are down roughly 95% and 99% from their peaks. The companies involved deny any improper arrangements.

Coffeezilla says he contacted Donald Trump, Melania, Eric and Donald Jr. before publishing and received no responses.

Worth noting for this industry: 

questions about officials’ crypto holdings are also one of the reasons the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate. Both sides of this are now on the record.

#Coffeezilla #WorldLiberty #CryptoRegulation #Web3 #USD1 #Binance #DigitalAssets

posts.title: CRYPTO COMPLIANCE HAS A DATA PROBLEM. MORE ALERTS WILL NOT NECESSARILY PRODUCE MORE INTELLIGENCE.
posts.author: RODRICK NDE CHINJE
posts.snippet:
CRYPTO COMPLIANCE HAS A DATA PROBLEM. MORE ALERTS WILL NOT NECESSARILY PRODUCE MORE INTELLIGENCE.
On 12 November, the Wolfsberg Group published new guidance following a workshop with the Basel Institute on Governance, bringing together financial institutions, regulators, financial intelligence units and cryptoasset service providers.
Its message is important for the future of institutional digital-asset adoption:
Suspicious activity reports should be judged by their intelligence value—not their volume.
The report identifies eight practical priorities:
Alerts and risk scores should trigger investigation, not automatically justify a report.
Institutions should explain why activity is suspicious and how evidence supports that conclusion.
Transaction identifiers and wallet information must be accurate and machine-readable.
Blockchain analytics should complement customer due diligence and behavioural analysis.
Analytics providers need stronger standards for governance, transparency and explainability.
Banks, crypto platforms and authorities need better information-sharing mechanisms.
Financial intelligence units should provide feedback and typology guidance.
Historical transaction tracing should be proportionate to the actual risk.
This exposes a structural weakness in many compliance systems.
A platform can generate thousands of alerts and still fail to explain which activity represents meaningful financial crime risk.
The next generation of digital-asset compliance must connect on-chain evidence, customer context, transaction behaviour and institutional intelligence into a coherent decision process.
For emerging markets, this is especially relevant as banks and regulated crypto businesses begin building deeper relationships.
At Core Intelligence™, we see the opportunity in moving from fragmented alerts to explainable, evidence-based financial intelligence.
The competitive advantage in compliance will not belong to institutions that generate the most alerts. It will belong to those that identify, explain and act on the right signals.
Are financial institutions investing enough in intelligence quality—or are they still measuring compliance performance by the volume of alerts and reports?
Source: The Wolfsberg Group, 12 November 2026
https://lnkd.in/esrK47Wz
posts.reason: Substantive discussion of crypto compliance standards and financial intelligence from Wolfsberg Group directly speaks to their compliance-officer and CASP-authorisation buyer segments.

comments.text: This lines up with what we see on the legal opinion side of token classification work - a report that flags a wallet without explaining why the pattern is suspicious gives a FIU nothing to act on, and under MiCAR's transparency expectations that gap will increasingly be treated as a control failure, not just a data problem.

Do you think FIUs are actually resourced to give the kind of typology feedback the Wolfsberg report calls for, or does that recommendation assume a maturity level most jurisdictions haven't reached yet?

We've had CASP applicants come to us with SAR processes built purely around alert volume, and the first question a regulator asks is always 'why is this suspicious,' not 'how many flags fired' - this guidance is a useful nudge in the right direction.

posts.title: 13 November 2026 | Policy • Banking • Financial Regulation • AI Innovation
posts.author: Shyam V.
posts.snippet:
13 November 2026 | Policy • Banking • Financial Regulation • AI Innovation

The UK financial services sector continues to evolve as regulators balance economic growth, financial stability, technological innovation and consumer protection.

Here are five developments shaping the industry:

1. FCA – Smarter Financial Regulation
The FCA’s November regulatory update reinforces data-led supervision, stronger market intelligence and proportionate regulation. Financial institutions must strengthen operational resilience, financial crime controls and consumer protection while reducing unnecessary compliance friction.

2. Banking Regulation & SM&CR Reforms
The FCA and PRA are consulting on simplifying the Senior Managers & Certification Regime. Proposed reforms could reduce compliance costs, streamline senior appointments and improve operational efficiency while retaining individual accountability.

3. Crypto & Digital Finance
The UK’s forthcoming cryptoasset regulatory framework is progressing, with authorisation applications opening ahead of the October 2027 regime. Banks and financial institutions should prepare for enhanced safeguarding, governance and financial resilience requirements.

4. AI, Automation & Financial Innovation
The FCA’s October AI good and poor practice publication highlights three priorities:

* Responsible AI governance and accountability.
* Explainability, fairness and consumer protection.
* Operational resilience and continuous monitoring.

For AI developers, opportunities are growing across KYC/CDD, AML transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, client onboarding, regulatory reporting and intelligent workflow automation.

5. Implications for Banks & Financial Professionals
The next competitive advantage will come from combining strong capital discipline, reliable data, effective risk management and responsible AI implementation.

Banks must invest in technology without compromising trust, regulatory compliance or human oversight.

My perspective:

The future of banking will not be determined by technology alone. It will depend on how effectively financial institutions integrate AI, regulatory intelligence, client servicing and operational expertise.

The opportunity is to move from reactive compliance towards predictive, data-driven and continuously monitored financial services.

Innovation must accelerate. Governance must evolve. Trust must remain fundamental.

#UKFinance #Banking #FCA #PRA #FinancialRegulation #ArtificialIntelligence #FinTech #KYC #AML #ClientOnboarding #OperationalResilience #InvestmentBanking #DigitalTransformation
posts.reason: UK financial regulation update with dedicated section on cryptoasset framework and October 2027 regime clearly relevant to their CASP-authorisation buyer urgency.

comments.text: Worth underlining on point 3: an FCA authorisation under the new cryptoasset regime is not a rubber stamp on top of existing VASP registration, it is a fresh test of governance, safeguarding and financial resilience, and firms that treat it as a formality are the ones stalling in the application queue.

Given how much weight point 4 puts on AI governance for KYC and transaction monitoring, do you think the FCA will treat AI Act-style risk tiering as a reference point even though it isn't bound by it post-Brexit?

We work across the EU on CASP and MiCA matters and the pattern Shyam describes in point 3 mirrors what we see with EU VASPs facing the 1 July 2026 transitional deadline - the authorisation bar is higher than people expect.

posts.title: One line from a press release last week stuck with me: on-chain lending has to serve more than crypto-native borrowers.
posts.author: Bharti Verma
posts.snippet:
One line from a press release last week stuck with me: on-chain lending has to serve more than crypto-native borrowers.

Cap, an on-chain credit marketplace, just financed a film. The loan is an advance against expected film production tax credits, guaranteed by independent underwriters who lock their own collateral on-chain.

At the same time, tokenized private credit on Solana has reached $1.44B, and credit tokens from Securitize and Maple are now accepted as collateral on Kamino (The Block).

Three things I notice:

1. Real-world borrowers are arriving: film, trade, receivables.
2. Credit tokens are becoming collateral, so the RWA and DeFi stacks are merging.
3. Underwriting and risk transparency will decide who earns trust.

Private credit is where I expect the next big RWA wave to come from. Do you agree, or is it still too opaque for on-chain?

#RWA #PrivateCredit #Tokenization #DeFi #OnchainFinance #Web3
posts.reason: Strong discussion of real-world credit tokenization and RWA which touches on their token classification and MiCA practice, and the author invites substantive debate on a topic relevant to their crypto-fintech clients.

comments.text: The merger you describe between RWA and DeFi stacks raises a classification question that gets skipped too often - once a credit token is pledged as collateral on a protocol like Kamino, whether it still functions as a simple debt instrument or starts looking like a transferable security depends heavily on the rights attached, not the label on the token.

When underwriters lock their own collateral on-chain as a guarantee, as with the Cap film loan, who do you see as actually bearing counterparty risk if the underlying tax credit falls through - the protocol, the underwriter, or the lender?

We've reviewed tokenomics for a number of asset-referenced and utility structures, and private credit is exactly where the line between a payment token and a security-like instrument gets tested hardest - transparency on underwriting is doing a lot of work in your argument.

FCA Proposes Major Updates to the Financial Crime Guide (CP26/38)

The FCA has just released a crucial consultation paper aimed at modernizing how regulated firms tackle financial crime. With evolving threats across multiple sectors, the proposed updates target several critical areas:

- Fraud: Expanded guidance focusing on APP fraud, money mules, and inter-departmental collaboration.
- Cryptoassets & Tech: Aligning expectations with upcoming regimes and integrating AI/third-party tool considerations.
- Sanctions & Proliferation: Tighter controls around screening, governance, and trade/export risks.

Consultation closes on December 24, 2026. Time for compliance and risk teams to review their systems and controls!

posts.title: Last week Microsoft announced that Anthropic models in Microsoft Copilot will be brought inside the EU Data Boundary.
posts.author: Eoin Fahy
posts.snippet:
Last week Microsoft announced that Anthropic models in Microsoft Copilot will be brought inside the EU Data Boundary.
 
For the regulated and risk-averse clients we work with, this was the moment they’d been waiting for. Law firms rejoiced... and then, as law firms do, they read the fine print.
 
Hidden in the announcement was one minor detail. This doesn’t apply to the UK.
 
Better yet, Anthropic models will be switched on automatically for UK tenants on 9 December unless an admin has turned them off. Lovely stuff.
 
For some organisations this won’t matter. But if you handle sensitive data that can’t be processed outside the UK or Europe because of policy, regulation or contractual obligations, this could put you in breach without anyone having made a decision.
 
Fret not, you can turn it off in a few steps..
 
1) Sign in to the Microsoft 365 admin centre as a Global Administrator and go to Copilot > Settings
2) Open “AI providers operating as Microsoft subprocessors”
3) Select “Disable Anthropic as a Microsoft subprocessor” and save
4) Go back to bed as Outlook is down
 
There’s a good case for using Claude models. They’re fantastic, after all. But this is a risk decision, not a tech decision.

275 Years: Peter, Palmer, Marc & Ben

Introduction: An Apology to the Gatekeepers

I owe you an apology.
Before we begin, I apologize to the venture funds, the endowments, the think tanks, the private equity partners, and the quiet rooms of Sand Hill Road and Wall Street for writing this book. I know the unwritten rules of the American upper class, and I am breaking all of them on page one.

To enter the business 1% in America, you must sign a silent non-disclosure agreement with history. You are expected to praise the market as a pure, colorblind meritocracy. You are expected to treat 275 years of State Sponsored authoritarianism against Black skin as a foreign disease—something that happened in Stalin’s Moscow or Mao’s Beijing, never in Charleston, Montgomery, or the boardrooms that financed them. Above all, if you get close to elite capital, you are never supposed to expose how the lock was built or who holds the key.
By writing this critique—and by naming the modern architects who turned closed networks into an ideology—I am forfeiting my own ticket to that club. I accept the punishment: the closed doors, the unreturned calls, the quiet blacklisting from the rooms where generational wealth is allocated. If undermining my own personal elite opportunities is the price required to leave an honest record and make this world better, I pay it willingly.

Why 275 Years?
Because from 1619 through the fall of Jim Crow in the mid-twentieth century, Black Americans lived under 275 years of Black state-sponsored authoritarianism. Every tool of totalitarian control that intellectuals at places like Stanford’s Hoover Institution condemn in Stalin’s Soviet Union—internal passports, forced labor camps, state surveillance, confiscated property, and the total denial of legal personhood—was practiced on American soil, backed by American courts, and monetized by American capital.

Yet when modern Silicon Valley titans—Peter Thiel, Palmer Luckey, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz—preach "techno-optimism," "American dynamism," and pure "meritocracy," they erase those 275 years of Black state-sponsored authoritarianism as if the race started yesterday on a clean track.
Worse, they lie about how they cleared the gatekeepers.

No openly gay man has ever moved through the American class system from zero to multi-billionaire. Peter Thiel reached the summit of global capital because he stayed in the closet—passing as straight inside Stanford Law, Wall Street, and early Silicon Valley until he had banked billions and could survive being outed. He moved through the dominant power structure in disguise, locked in permanent institutional protection, and then turned around to declare that identity doesn't matter and that diversity efforts are "evil."

That is the ultimate asymmetry of American power: a white gay man can hide in plain sight to enter the upper wealth class; a Black person cannot fake their skin color while asking for seed capital.
Today, the state and the market offer Black America a two-tiered bargain: "As the State, systemically we won’t hurt all of you—especially those of you who assimilate, play by the rules of the dominant class, or join the 1,500 Black families worth over $50 million." Those 1,500 families are held up as proof that the ledger is clean.

It is not. Black Americans still do not possess American ideals, and the proof is written in the daily mechanics of law, property, and capital:
• No Equal Protection Under the Law: Over the last decade, American cities have poured more than $1.8 billion in taxpayer money into a state-sponsored slush fund to settle lawsuits for officers who assault, maim, and kill Black citizens—shielding the perpetrators behind qualified immunity while forcing Black taxpayers to fund the payouts for violence inflicted on their own communities.
• No Second Amendment in Practice: While the right to bear arms is treated as sacred for white citizens, legally armed Black men like Philando Castile and Amir Locke were executed by state agents within seconds, with zero criminal accountability.

• No Equal Access to Capital or Property: Black founders receive less than 1% of all venture capital deployed in America, while systemic appraisal bias strips hundreds of billions of dollars in generational equity from Black homeowners.
• No Equal Voice in the Republic: Surgical gerrymandering and targeted voting barriers routinely dilute Black political power whenever it threatens entrenched legislatures.

And here is the geopolitical consequence Washington and Silicon Valley refuse to face: when America denies Black people American ideals at home, it makes China attractive.

Beijing does not need to invent anti-American propaganda when America broadcasts its own hypocrisy every day. When Black founders are shut out of Sand Hill Road, when a $1.8 billion slush fund protects state violence, and when tech billionaires build surveillance empires while attacking civil rights, China steps into the vacuum. Beijing offers infrastructure capital across Africa and the diaspora without lectures on "meritocracy," opens state-backed trade doors to Black entrepreneurs, and points to America’s streets to argue that Western democracy is a lie. You cannot defeat Chinese authoritarianism abroad while running a two-tiered democracy at home.

Meanwhile, Peter, Palmer, Marc, and Ben pour billions into surveillance software, predictive policing data, and autonomous defense hardware that arm that exact same domestic state apparatus while lecturing the public that systemic racism is a myth.

This book is not a call to burn Capitalism; it is an indictment of erasing 275 years of authoritarianism-forget equality. It is an honest reckoning with 275 years of Black state-sponsored authoritarianism and modern racial capitalism—written at the cost of my own seat at the table—so that America finally delivers on its own ideals before its own citizens stop believing in them.

OpenForum Europe is part of the NGI Commons consortium organising the Digital Commons Policy Summit 2026, in close collaboration with the European Commission. The Summit brought together policymakers, regulators, funders and practitioners to help deliver on the ambitions of the Tech Sovereignty Package and the EU Open Source Strategy. 

OFE Executive Director Laszlo Igneczi spoke on the panel “Introducing the NGI Commons Strategic Agenda”, which explored the practical challenges and opportunities of operationalising Digital Commons at scale. The discussion addressed key issues around governance, coordination, financing, and implementation, while offering suggestions for translating the NGI Commons Strategic Agenda into concrete action. The panel was moderated by Paul Keller (Open Future Foundation), Plixavra Vogiatzoglou (University of Amsterdam’s Institute for Information Law – IViR) and Jan Penfrat (EDRi) were also speakers.

OFE Senior Policy Advisor Nicholas Gates moderated the panel “Commoners and Funding: Securing the Future”, which explored the evolving funding and support landscape for Digital Commons projects in Europe. Grounded in NGI Commons analysis and insights from practitioners, the discussion highlighted the successes and lessons learned from existing funding models, put forward recommendations for the FP10 and MFF phase, and explored how to ensure the long-term sustainability of Digital Commons funding. The panel also featured  Jorge Gasos (European Commission), Arnaud L.  (Consul Democracy), Rachel FOUCARD (TYPO3), Franziska B. (Sovereign Tech Agency), and Jean-François De Hertogh (Open Source Europe) as speakers.

Building on the success of the 2025 edition, which established Digital Commons as a key pillar of European Digital Sovereignty, the 2026 Digital Commons Policy Summit shifted the focus from introduction to implementation of the Tech Sovereignty Package. It empowered Digital Commons communities, deliver on the EU Open Source Strategy, and advance the NGI Commons Strategic Agenda to strengthen the role of Digital Commons in the new European Open Internet Stack.

I had the pleasure of joining our client Ronan Harris (Chief Commercial Officer at Snap Inc.) and moderator Massimo Marioni to unpack Mindscope's behavioural science study, Reset Velocity.

For the past decade, our industry has been obsessed with chasing passive attention, broad reach, and performative visibility. Now, people are retreating to what genuinely rewards their actual needs; and those needs have to be understood better.

The wonderful feedback and relevance of our insights was brilliant to see! Sharing three takeaways from the research and our conversation that brands need to carry into 2027:

→ The migration from public to private, high-trust environments. Amongst hyper-digital landscapes, people are gravitating toward private, genuine spaces to gain more personal agency over their environments and decisions. The law of polarity, more than ever. Hyper-tech grows = our internal locus of control grows evenly. 

→ Connection is the new currency; the relational economy. Drawing on social capital, self-determination, and dramaturgical theories, our research shows that the "back stage" drives far deeper influence than passive views can ever sustain.

→ Purchases compound beyond the main feed. Discovery happens in broader spaces, but actual purchasing decisions and brand affinity are shaped in everyday, communal conversations- where over half of brands are now asked to share more about their offering when close to purchase.

Why? Because once a system goes live, the cost of a mistake can be

No. ZRU-1125). Mandatory data localization applies, in particular, 
to biometric and genetic data, 
as well as data of users of telecommunications operators.

What should be considered in advance?

1️⃣Data minimization — collect and store only what is truly necessary. The less data you keep, the smaller your attack surface.
2️⃣Access control — RBAC, MFA, and the principle of least privilege help limit the consequences of account compromise.
3️⃣Encryption — protect data both 
at rest and in transit using modern cryptographic mechanisms, TLS, 
and secure key management.
4️⃣Logging and monitoring — it 
is important to know who accessed which data and when. SIEM and automated alerts help detect suspicious activity faster.
5️⃣Infrastructure 
security — network segmentation, backups, secure APIs, component updates, and regular vulnerability testing all help reduce security risks.

posts.title: A man flies home from Singapore to celebrate Diwali and attend a family wedding—and is shot dead by his own neighbor over a parking space.
posts.author: Divya Singh
posts.snippet:
A man flies home from Singapore to celebrate Diwali and attend a family wedding—and is shot dead by his own neighbor over a parking space.  

​The CCTV footage from Faridabad of former Tech Mahindra business head Paramjeet Dhankhar’s final moments is deeply unsettling. Not just because of the brutality of the act, but because of what triggered it: an everyday dispute over car parking in a residential building in Delhi-NCR.

​It forces us to ask some uncomfortable questions about where we are heading as a society:

​1. Where is all this pent-up rage coming from?
We are living in an increasingly fast-paced, high-pressure environment where patience is wearing dangerously thin. When everyday frustrations boil over into lethal violence, something is fundamentally broken in how we handle conflict and regulate our emotions.

​2. The danger isn't always a stranger.
We often worry about external threats, yet data and reality repeatedly show that extreme harm frequently comes from people we know—neighbors, acquaintances, people sharing the exact same spaces. When basic trust and neighborly empathy disappear, no gated community or metro city is truly safe.

​3. Accountability and gun laws matter.
The accused reportedly used a licensed firearm. While the police made a swift arrest, we have to ask why minor neighborhood disputes escalate unchecked and how strictly psychological fitness and accountability are enforced before issuing gun licenses.  

​This isn't a problem unique to India—gun violence and civic anger are global crises. But as a nation aiming to lead on the world stage, our ambitions mean very little if we lose our basic humanity along the way. True progress isn't just measured in GDP or corporate titles; it is measured by whether two neighbors can resolve a disagreement without destroying two families.

​We need stronger preventive policing, stricter scrutiny on firearms, and—more than anything—a collective pause to rethink what this constant state of anger is costing us.

posts.title: Everyone talks about the funnel. TOFU, MOFU, BOFU.
posts.author: Viraj Sutar
posts.snippet:
Everyone talks about the funnel. TOFU, MOFU, BOFU.

Very few people explain what to actually do with it.

So here's the simple version.

It's one buyer making three kinds of searches. The words they type tell you which stage they're in.

TOFU, top of the funnel. They have a question.

▪ Searches start with: what, how, why

▪ Example: "how to track sales leads"

▪ Give them: a how-to guide or a blog post that answers it fully. No sales pitch yet.

MOFU, middle of the funnel. They're comparing options.

▪ Searches include: best, top, vs, alternatives, review

▪ Example: "best CRM for startups"

▪ Give them: a comparison page, a "best tools" list or a case study.

BOFU, bottom of the funnel. They're ready to buy.

▪ Searches include: pricing, cost, demo, free trial, buy

▪ Example: "CRM pricing"

▪ Give them: a pricing page, a demo page and a short contact form.

How to use this on your own site

▪ Take your keyword list, or export your queries from Search Console.

▪ Tag every keyword T, M or B, based on the words in it.

▪ Count how many pages you have for each stage.

If most of your pages are T and almost none are B, that's your gap.

If I had to pick one place to start, I'd start at the bottom. Fewer people search those terms, but they're the closest to buying.

That's also why my 60-day SEO plan has the core pages first and only 2 blog posts, right at the end.

One note: this is a rule of thumb, not a law. "How much does a CRM cost" starts with how, but that person is at the bottom.

Do just this much and you'll know what to write next.

Which stage has the fewest pages on your site right now?

posts.title: Thanks to Dimitris for highlighting this critical DNV safety notice regarding the Nishi-F FF-65 free-fall lifeboats.
posts.author: DEEPAK SODHI
posts.snippet:
Thanks to Dimitris for highlighting this critical DNV safety notice regarding the Nishi-F FF-65 free-fall lifeboats. 

Seeing a structural issue—like a 70-90 mm passage width shortage—flagged on lifeboats manufactured from October 2010 onwards begs a larger industry question: *Why do these major discrepancies suddenly surface after so many years in service?*

How does a static, physical measurement issue pass initial yard deliveries, sea trials, and over a decade of annual class and PSC inspections before becoming a fleet-wide deficiency? 

Cases like this are a stark reminder of a few realities in vessel management:

1️⃣ The 'Hidden in Plain Sight' Effect: Latent design or construction defects can easily be grandfathered in during initial delivery and subsequent surveys simply because earlier inspections assumed the baseline manufacturer specs met the LSA Code.

2️⃣ Evolving Audit Lenses: What passes during a vessel's first few years often faces much tighter scrutiny later on. It usually takes a single incident, a tightened regulatory focus, or one incredibly diligent inspector to shatter the status quo and trigger a retroactive DNV safety notice.

3️⃣ Baseline Trust vs. Verification: We often rely heavily on the initial OEM and yard certifications. A 480 mm minimum requirement under LSA Code 4.7.2.1 is black and white, yet it took years to flag a 70-90 mm discrepancy.

This is a great reminder that 'approved at delivery' doesn't mean we stop looking critically at our legacy systems. Proactive lifecycle management means constantly verifying what we assume is already compliant. 

Has your fleet had to manage retroactive compliance issues like this on older tonnage? Let's discuss in the comments. 👇

posts.title: 🤔 AI may not need to copy your work to destroy its commercial value. And copyright law may have surprisingly little to say about it.
posts.author: Nikol Ullmann
posts.snippet:
🤔 AI may not need to copy your work to destroy its commercial value. And copyright law may have surprisingly little to say about it.

On 3 November 2026, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar delivered his Opinion in Case C-250/25, Like Company v Google Ireland, the first generative AI case before the Court of Justice of the European Union.

At first glance, another copyright dispute involving AI. On closer examination, something considerably more consequential.

The Opinion draws a crucial distinction between training an AI model, retrieving protected content and reproducing that content in an AI-generated answer.

While the Advocate General considers LLM training generally capable of benefiting from the EU’s text and data mining exception, subject to its conditions, real-time retrieval and reuse of press publications may infringe publishers’ rights where access restrictions are circumvented or protected expression is recognisably reproduced.

But the most intellectually challenging issue lies elsewhere.

❓ What if an AI system extracts the informational value of an article so effectively that no one needs to read the original, while reproducing none of its protected expression?

Copyright protects expression, not facts. Economic substitution, however substantial, does not automatically establish infringement.

This creates a fascinating regulatory asymmetry. An AI-generated answer may be legally permissible precisely because it is sufficiently different from its source, even while competing with that source for the same audience.

There is another important dimension. The Advocate General’s approach connects potential provider liability to system design, business models and the effectiveness of safeguards against infringement.

In other words, copyright compliance is becoming an architectural question, not merely a contractual one.

For me, the deepest question is:
 
❓If AI becomes the primary consumer of original journalism, while humans increasingly consume only AI-generated answers, who will finance the production of the information on which those answers depend?
 
This is not simply a copyright question. It concerns the economic sustainability of knowledge production, media pluralism and the future structure of the information economy.
 
The Court has yet to rule. Whatever the outcome, the implications extend far beyond Google Gemini.

Read here the Advocate General’s Opinion, 3 November 2026, C-250/25: https://lnkd.in/d8A-83P2

🇸🇪 SWEDEN: TRANSPARENCY IS NOT A PROMISE. IT IS A RIGHT.

What if citizens could access government documents without having to explain why?

Sweden has embraced this principle since 1766, when it introduced one of the world’s earliest laws guaranteeing access to official information.

Three important lessons:

OPENNESS: Public information should be accessible by default.

ACCOUNTABILITY: Government decisions must be open to scrutiny.

PUBLIC TRUST: Transparency makes institutions more credible and strengthens democracy.

Of course, legitimate exceptions exist. But secrecy should never become the default.

My key takeaway:

A government should never fear informed citizens. It should welcome them.

posts.snippet:
💙 Novembro Azul é muito mais do que falar de câncer de próstata.

É um convite para olhar a saúde do homem de forma mais completa: pressão arterial, colesterol, diabetes, sono, peso, atividade física, vacinação, saúde mental, rastreamentos e acompanhamento médico.

Muitas vezes, o maior problema não é uma doença específica, é o hábito de adiar cuidado, minimizar sintomas e buscar ajuda só quando a situação já saiu do controle.

E sim, a próstata faz parte dessa conversa. Mas prevenção de verdade não é uma fórmula igual para todo mundo. Ela depende de idade, sintomas, história familiar e risco individual.

Também vale lembrar que saúde mental é saúde. Ansiedade, depressão, exaustão, insônia e sofrimento emocional não devem ser tratados como fraqueza ou ignorados em silêncio.

🧬 A genética também pode entrar nessa história, especialmente quando existem padrões familiares de câncer, cardiopatias, morte súbita ou outras condições hereditárias. Mas ela é só uma parte do cuidado: o resto envolve hábitos, acompanhamento e decisões do dia a dia.

Talvez a melhor mensagem deste Novembro Azul seja esta: não espere um problema grande para começar a cuidar da sua saúde.

Behind every patent is someone who spent years chasing an idea, and behind every trade mark is a business that bet its name on something new. Yesterday, that spirit filled the room at Fundación PONS in #Madrid, where we welcomed a delegation from the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) for an open and generous exchange on how intangible assets are protected and managed in Europe and Spain.

CNIPA is the authority behind one of the largest innovation systems in the world. In 2025 alone, it received 1,927,500 invention patent applications, a year-on-year increase of 5.43%. Foreign applicants filed around 94,000 trade mark applications in China in the first half of 2025 alone, up 7.4%. And Chinese applicants grew their international patent filings through the PCT system by 12.7% over the same period, a sign of how far innovation now travels. Figures like these show that intangible assets are no longer a niche concern: they shape how companies compete, grow and build trust across borders.

The conversation went to the heart of what protection means in practice: how administrative and judicial routes connect, how specialised IP courts work, and where mediation and arbitration fit alongside litigation. These are questions our clients bring to us every day, often from very different starting points, and it meant a great deal to hear them discussed with such candour.

Three members of our team took part. Guillermo Criado, director of International Business Development, spoke about the many #SMEs in Spain and Europe whose most valuable creations remain unprotected, and about why registration should be the start of a strategy, not the end of one. Isabel Cortes Martinez director of Institucional and International Projects presented #ScaleLab, the programme we have run since 2025 as an Entidad de Enlace de Innovación Tecnológica for the Comunidad de Madrid, which offers free advice, training and events to local SMEs and startups with ambition. Elisa Monte, IP lawyer specialising in licensing and technology transfer, showed how intangible assets are valued, and how that valuation turns a good idea into a deal, a licence or an investment.

#China and Spain build their IP systems differently, but they share the same aspirations: rights that can be enforced, disputes that get resolved efficiently, and knowledge that becomes lasting value for the people who created it. Meetings like this one bring those aspirations closer.

Thank you to the CNIPA delegation for their time, their openness and a conversation we will not forget. We look forward to continuing it 😊 👍

posts.title: Consultoría externa ante relaciones conflictivas crónicas en el Comité de Dirección
posts.author: Sergi Vilardell
posts.snippet:
Consultoría externa ante relaciones conflictivas crónicas en el Comité de Dirección

Hay conflictos que forman parte de la vida normal de un comité de dirección: desacuerdos sobre estrategia, prioridades o recursos, que se discuten, se deciden y se cierran. Y hay otros que no se cierran nunca. Se prolongan durante años, sobreviven a las reestructuraciones y a los cambios de responsabilidades, y acaban formando parte del paisaje. Todos los miembros del comité saben que existen, y casi nadie habla de ellos abiertamente. 
Un conflicto crónico se reconoce menos por su intensidad que por su persistencia. Reaparece en temas que aparentemente no tienen relación entre sí, se reactiva ante cualquier decisión importante y condiciona alianzas, silencios y formas de votar. Con el tiempo, el comité aprende a funcionar a su alrededor: se evitan determinados temas, se preparan las reuniones para que no estallen y algunas decisiones se toman fuera de la mesa. El coste rara vez aparece en un informe, pero se paga en lentitud, en decisiones que no se toman y en equipos que perciben la tensión de arriba aunque nadie la nombre. 
Cuando un conflicto se repite de esta manera, conviene dejar de leerlo como un problema entre dos personas. Lo que se repite suele ocupar el lugar de algo que no se está pudiendo decir. Una sucesión que nadie plantea, una autoridad que nunca terminó de definirse o un acuerdo de origen que ya no se sostiene encuentran en el enfrentamiento entre dos directivos su única forma de expresión. Y en las rivalidades prolongadas suele ocurrir que cada parte ve en la otra, con toda nitidez, aquello que no soporta de sí misma. Por eso los argumentos racionales no alcanzan: el conflicto no se sostiene en la falta de información, sino en lo que cada uno pone en juego en él. 
Desde dentro, esta lectura es casi imposible. Cada miembro del comité forma parte de la dinámica que intenta resolver, tiene una posición que proteger y una versión de los hechos que defender. Tampoco la presidencia está fuera: con frecuencia, el conflicto se organiza precisamente en torno a su lugar.
Ahí reside el sentido de una mirada externa. No para arbitrar ni para dictar quién tiene razón, porque ocupar ese lugar solo reproduciría el conflicto con un actor más. Su valor está en ofrecer a cada miembro un espacio donde pueda decir lo que no se dice en la mesa, sin las lealtades ni los riesgos que operan dentro. A partir de ahí, la pregunta deja de ser quién es el responsable y pasa a ser qué parte tiene cada uno en lo que está ocurriendo. Es ese desplazamiento el que permite que el comité vuelva a discutir sobre el negocio y no sobre lo que se callaba.
Un comité de dirección no necesita eliminar el desacuerdo, que es parte de su función. Necesita que deje de ocupar el lugar de lo que no se está hablando.

En Clínica Viher acompañamos a comités de dirección y órganos de gobierno en situaciones de conflicto prolongado, con total confidencialidad.

posts.title: Gestionar el cambio: transformar requiere más que una decisión
posts.author: Peggy Torres
posts.snippet:
Gestionar el cambio: transformar requiere más que una decisión

Cambiar es una decisión. Transformarse es un proceso.

Y aunque muchas organizaciones reconocen la necesidad de evolucionar, no siempre están preparadas para afrontar todo lo que implica hacerlo.

La gestión del cambio no consiste simplemente en introducir nuevas herramientas, modificar procesos o establecer objetivos diferentes. Supone cuestionar formas de hacer las cosas, abandonar prácticas conocidas, aprender nuevas maneras de trabajar y, sobre todo, desarrollar la capacidad de avanzar incluso cuando no tenemos todas las respuestas.

Toda transformación atraviesa momentos de incertidumbre. Aparecen resistencias, surgen dificultades, se alteran dinámicas de trabajo y, en ocasiones, aquello que parecía estar bajo control entra en una etapa de desorganización.

Es precisamente allí donde comienza uno de los mayores desafíos: aprender a gestionar el caos sin perder de vista el propósito.

Transformarse exige resiliencia, flexibilidad y una enorme capacidad de adaptación. Requiere equipos dispuestos a aprender, líderes capaces de escuchar y organizaciones que comprendan que los resultados no aparecen de manera inmediata.

También exige reconocer que cada avance tiene un proceso detrás. Hay decisiones que corregir, estrategias que ajustar, errores que comprender y aprendizajes que incorporar. No todos los pasos serán lineales ni todos los resultados llegarán en el tiempo esperado.

Por eso, gestionar el cambio implica acompañar a las personas, fortalecer sus capacidades, construir confianza y generar las condiciones necesarias para que la transformación no se quede en una intención, sino que pueda convertirse en una realidad sostenible.

En Open Way – Consultoría Internacional entendemos que transformar no significa tener todas las respuestas desde el principio. Significa desarrollar las herramientas para interpretar los desafíos, actuar con criterio, aprender durante el proceso y encontrar nuevas posibilidades incluso en escenarios complejos.

Porque el cambio no siempre comienza en condiciones perfectas. A veces comienza precisamente cuando comprendemos que necesitamos hacer las cosas de otra manera.

Transformarse requiere valentía para comenzar, resiliencia para continuar y visión para reconocer hacia dónde queremos avanzar.

posts.snippet: $178M in long positions was liquidated inside one hour after the October US CPI print came in above forecast, per Cointelegraph. Traders read that as volatility. For a comms team it is a scheduling failure. The first hour after a macro release is the cheapest attention crypto ever gets. Search demand spikes, every timeline is open, and almost nobody has a checkable fact in hand. That asymmetry is the opportunity: the audience wants context and the market is supplying opinions. What most teams actually do with it: open a doc at the print, chase an executive for a quote, wait on legal, publish 5 hours later - a thread of guesses with no number in it. The volatility is gone by then. The guess is not. A wrong directional call gets screenshotted and quoted back for a year. Call it the Pre-Cleared Macro Page. Three steps for a head of growth: 1. Draft the page before the print. Three plain lines on how your product behaves when rates move - collateral, funding, spreads, redemptions, whatever is actually true for you. No scenarios you cannot support. 2. Put in one number only you can publish, from your own dashboard, with a date on it. Your own data is the one thing nobody else can post in that hour. 3. Pre-approve the template with legal and write the prediction ban into it. The template is approved once; individual posts then ship in 15 minutes. Fail mode: if your product has no genuine exposure to rates, this backfires. The page reads as a project renting someone else's news, and the next time you have something real, the feed has already priced you as noise. The cost of getting this wrong is not a missed post. It is handing your highest-demand hour of the quarter to a guess that outlives the move. What does your team have pre-written for the next CPI print?

CHAIN, Part 4: INTAKE, How NGOs can actually find crypto donors

A donation policy and a wallet are important.

But neither raises a single donation on its own.

I see this as a five-step process.

1️⃣ MAP : Identify potential donors

Start with publicly available information.

Potential audiences include individual crypto holders, philanthropic foundations, Web3 grant programs, company treasuries and blockchain communities.

The objective isn't to contact everyone.

It's to identify people and institutions whose interests genuinely align with your mission.

Respect privacy and avoid intrusive donor profiling.

2️⃣ OFFER : Explain the value of supporting your mission

A wallet address is not a fundraising strategy.

Potential donors need to understand:

* What problem are you addressing? 
* What measurable outcome are you targeting?
* How will the contribution be used?
* How will you report on its use?

A dedicated public receiving wallet and quarterly reporting can help establish transparency.

But blockchain visibility alone is not proof of impact. The organization must connect transactions to actual expenditure and results. 

3️⃣ ASK :  Make the request concrete

Replace generic requests such as "Any amount helps" with specific funding opportunities.

Explain the activity, the target beneficiaries, the expected outcome and the reporting commitment.

A credible request makes it easier for a donor to understand what their contribution will support. 

4️⃣ Close. Clear instructions, then your compliance gate before the money moves, then a fast thank-you and receipt. 

5️⃣ Steward. Report back with evidence. A donor who sees impact gives again.

A donor who receives credible evidence of impact has a stronger reason to support the organization again.

💢 My view: Trust is the real fundraising infrastructure.

The NGO that succeeds in crypto fundraising won't necessarily be the one with the most sophisticated blockchain technology or the most attractive donation page.

It will be the one that is easiest to trust.

Compliance, transparency and clear reporting should not be treated as administrative obstacles.

They are part of the fundraising proposition.

Respect donor anonymity requests and ensure that applicable legal, tax, donor and internal-control requirements are addressed. These rules differ by country and funder, so obtain qualified advice.

📌 Save this five-step framework if your organization is exploring crypto donations.

Comment CHAIN and I'll share the one-page donor intake playbook.

For NGO leaders and fundraising professionals: What is the biggest obstacle to attracting crypto donors: credibility, compliance, donor discovery or impact reporting?

This is my own analysis and opinion, not investment advice. Do your own research and make your own decisions.

BREAKING: Louisiana Takes Aim at the Entire Prediction Market Industry

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill has reportedly launched a sweeping state-court enforcement action targeting 10 major prediction market operators and intermediaries: Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto*com, Coinbase, Novig, Underdog, Gemini Titan, ForecastEx and ProphetX.

The state is seeking an emergency temporary restraining order barring sports, awards, political and election event contracts.

One lawsuit. Ten defendants. An entire industry in the crosshairs.

If confirmed, Louisiana's action would mark a significant escalation in the nationwide legal battle over prediction markets.

Louisiana would become the 13th state to pursue civil enforcement against prediction market operators. An unlucky number for an industry already fighting state regulators on multiple fronts.

But the number isn't the biggest story.

The real significance is Louisiana's proposed enforcement strategy.

Rather than pursuing individual platforms through separate cease-and-desist letters and lawsuits, the state would be targeting virtually the entire field in a single proceeding.

No more regulatory whack-a-mole.

One case. All the major players.

And the implications extend well beyond whether these platforms can continue offering sports-related event contracts.

Louisiana is reportedly seeking restitution, disgorgement and civil penalties. Those remedies could expose the industry to financial liability for past transactions, not merely restrictions on future operations.

Consider the potential consequences if the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately determines that federal commodities law does not preempt state gambling regulation of sports event contracts.

Shutting down sports contracts could prove to be the least of the industry's worries.

The potential financial exposure from restitution, disgorgement and civil penalties across multiple states could be staggering.

Nor would aggressive enforcement be out of character for Louisiana.

AG Liz Murrill and Gaming Division Director Dawn Himel have been at the forefront of the state's efforts to combat unlawful gambling. Louisiana has also distinguished itself through its attorney general's formal legal opinion addressing sweepstakes casinos.

Louisiana's approach also marks a significant departure from the piecemeal enforcement strategies employed elsewhere. Rather than sending cease-and-desist letters that effectively invite operators to race into federal court, the state has taken the offensive, bringing the major players into a single state-court proceeding. Other states could achieve a similar result through simultaneous enforcement actions.

Veterans, active-duty service members, and their families are frequently targeted by financial scams, losing hundreds of millions of dollars each year (with reported losses reaching $685 million).
The most prevalent and damaging scams include:

1. "Claims Sharks" and Predatory Benefits Companies

• What it is: Unaccredited consultants or fraudulent companies (sometimes called "claims sharks") charge veterans high upfront fees, monthly subscriptions, or a percentage of future payouts to help file or expedite initial Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) disability claims. They often falsely guarantee a higher disability rating.
• The Reality: Filing a VA disability claim is 100% free. You should only work with accredited representatives (such as VSOs, attorneys, or claims agents) recognized by the VA. You can verify credentials using the VA Office of the General Counsel Accreditation Search.

2. VA Overpayment & Impostor Scams

• What it is: Scammers spoof phone numbers, emails, or texts pretending to be VA officials, claiming the veteran received a benefit overpayment. They demand immediate payment via gift cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfers, or prepaid cards to avoid legal trouble or benefit freezes.
• The Reality: The VA will send official written notices via mail for benefit adjustments—they will never demand instant payment over the phone or via gift cards/crypto.

3. Pension Poaching

• What it is: Scammers target older veterans (65+) and their families by offering to restructure or "hide" assets to help them quickly qualify for VA Aid and Attendance pension benefits. In reality, these schemes lock veterans into high-risk annuities, risky investments, or outright theft of their nest eggs.

4. Education Benefit (GI Bill) Scams

• What it is: Unaccredited or predatory for-profit "degree mills" target veterans with promises of fast-track certificates or degrees tailored to drain GI Bill housing and tuition allowances while providing little to no real academic value.

5. VA Home Loan Scams

• What it is: Phony lenders or mortgage brokers contact veterans offering "special" refinancing terms, skip-a-payment deals, or lower rates, often slipping in hidden fee increases, cash-out traps, or deceptive deed transfers.

6. Bogus Military Charities and Phishing

• What it is: Fake charities impersonate well-known veteran support foundations to solicit immediate donations. Similarly, phishing emails or texts try to trick veterans into handing over Social Security numbers, bank logins, or service records.
• The Reality: You can check the legitimacy of any charity through tools like Charity navigator.

A Presidency of Corruption? Public Office, Private Profit, and Public Trust
In earlier posts, I raised questions about market activity around geopolitical events and the uncertainty created by political decisions. A related concern is the boundary between public power and private business.
The Associated Press reported that the Trump Organization completed eight overseas deals during the first year of Donald Trump’s second term, compared with none during his first. AP also reported that, shortly before the inauguration, the Trump family sold nearly half of its World Liberty Financial crypto business to a UAE government-linked company for $500 million. A separate UAE government fund later invested $2 billion in Binance using a stablecoin issued by World Liberty. The administration subsequently reversed a restriction and granted the UAE access to advanced U.S. chips. AP said it is difficult to know whether the business deals played any role in that policy outcome. The White House says Trump has no conflicts of interest and is not involved in family deals. The timing warrants scrutiny, but does not by itself prove a quid pro quo.
A June 2026 Reuters investigation estimated that the Trump family had gained at least $2.3 billion from its main crypto ventures since Trump returned to office. Reuters also estimated that more than one million investors had net losses totaling $2.3 billion by the end of April; that figure includes paper losses on unsold holdings.
An AP-NORC poll published in October found that about six in ten U.S. adults believed Trump was either profiting illegally or acting unethically, though not illegally. That is a measure of public opinion, not a legal finding. Still, public confidence depends on clear safeguards when a president’s family has significant business interests.
Public office carries a duty to serve the public. Transparency, independent oversight, and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules matter because citizens must be able to trust that government decisions are made in the public interest.

posts.author: Gagan Chawla

​Bhai Dooj and a Sister’s Share: What Two 2026 Supreme Court Rulings Mean for Daughters’ Property Rights
​On Bhai Dooj, sisters apply tilak while brothers pledge lifelong protection. Yet when it comes to ancestral homes or inherited real estate, a crucial question often remains deferred: Does the sister’s name appear on the title deeds?  
​For families and NRIs managing legacy assets across Delhi NCR and PAN India, informal understandings or unilateral mutations frequently trigger protracted litigation. Under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a daughter—married or unmarried—holds rights equal to a son, both as a coparcener by birth (Section 6) and as a Class I heir in intestate succession (Section 8).  
​Two landmark 2026 Supreme Court rulings reinforce this protection:  
​🔹 B.S. Lalitha v. Bhuvanesh (May 2026 | 2026 INSC 499):
A partition deed executed solely among brothers does not automatically extinguish a sister’s pre-existing Section 8 inheritance rights. Section 6(5) is a trial defence that must be proved on evidence—not a summary bar against excluded daughters.  
​🔹 Darubai v. Kamalabai (June 2026 | 2026 INSC 613):
When property devolves under Section 8, Class I heirs hold definite shares as tenants-in-common. One heir cannot act as Karta to sell or mortgage another co-heir’s share without consent.  
​Key Takeaway for Families & NRIs:
Revenue mutation entries alone neither create nor extinguish legal title. Protecting family harmony requires transparent documentation—a duly stamped, registered Family Settlement or Partition Deed recording every Class I heir.

So this week OpenAI Foundation board member Paul Christiano told a room full of quivering devotees that “for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”

Apart from being a CBM (Certified Bruh Moment) of the most alarming kind – and my thoughts are with his comms team, who probably simultaneously smacked their foreheads so hard that seismic detectors in China started losing it – this really goes to a question in AI that comes up almost constantly in our conversations with other orgs.

Since we launched Prima Transform, our revolutionary AI workplace transformation methodology (yada yada yada – I know, stay with me), one of the key, and frankly most shocking, recurring questions has been one of risk ownership. Who owns AI?

You can’t delegate responsibility to AI. AI is not beholden to the law, company policy, or society’s standards. It is being developed and managed by massive shareholder-driven companies with so much debt on the books that Machiavelli is banging on his coffin, lunging for the chance to turn the Nvidia spy affair into an everyday fact of life. What little democratic oversight of AI’s development exists is stunningly thin and at the mercy of some of the most influential and well-funded powers in the world. And, of course, it’s all coming out of Trump’s America – and I’m sure we all have total faith in their responsible tech-sector oversight.

Who owns AI at your organisation? Or more specifically, whose scalp is in danger if your organisation misuses AI? 48% of AI users admit to ignoring their employer’s AI policy. If something goes wrong, and the Herald Sun – or a regulator – or Maurice Blackburn – or even the Federal Police hit up your board tomorrow and ask them to present on how you’ve been responsible with your AI rollout, well... this is when you would really like to have a better defence than hoping that the pen runs out of ink when they’re putting all the zeros on the fine you’ll need to pay.

To quote Michael Clayton, the greatest legal thriller of all time: the police don’t call. They just show up.

Policy isn’t governance. AI is the riskiest technology in the history of computing. If it all goes belly-up, you need something much stronger than meekly pointing at some module that you put your staff through when you rolled out the Please Blow Up Our Brand machine company-wide and expected them to figure it out themselves.

We are entering a glorious new Golden Age of Piracy – a legendary time, whispered about in hushed, giddy tones by North Korean hackers – where it has never been so easy to gut your tech security and put an ice pick through your brand’s cranium forever. I’m in the wrong business; I should be in ransomware attacks. It’s the new selling-shovels-in-a-gold-rush.

Unfortunately for me – and unlike AI – I am beholden to my ethics and the law. Are your AI agents? How do you enforce that? How do you prove that you’ve been doing so this whole time? And if it all goes wrong, how long will the stunned silence last on the other end of the phone when you have to call your lawyers?

And which lucky duck gets to tell the board?

posts.author: Torsten Kriening
posts.snippet:
THE KRIENING BRIEF - 11 November 2026
 
(1) Berlin, this morning. The 19th NewSpace Breakfast, at Reflex Aerospace. Walter Ballheimer set out what it would actually mean if the United States were no longer an ally.
 
Not that we go blind and deaf, he said. That we switch from a fibre broadband line back to a fax. “And even though we in Germany do know how to work a fax, that would still be a disadvantage.”
 
Europe can do all of it. Ariane, Vega, and now Isar from mainland Europe. Remote sensing. Communications. His point was the sentence before: we cannot do it well enough. Coverage, bandwidth, the sheer number of American satellites.
 
(2) Yesterday in SpaceWatch.Global, Gilles Rabin asked who seriously thought Germany could handle €35 billion in orders over five years with the same industry and the same national and military organisation.
 
This morning, Berlin answered him without meaning to.
 
Dr. Nils Schmid, parliamentary state secretary at the defence ministry, put it plainly: “These 35 billion are not simply a pot of money.” They are the planning figure for what the Bundeswehr calculates it needs by 2030. Asked how much of it is under contract, he said it is not, because the procedures are still running.
 
Then the clearance question. Companies may bid only once they are security cleared. The clearing authorities will clear them only once they hold a contract. The answer offered was that the Länder should hire more vetting staff at their own state intelligence services.
 
One founder in the room, dryly: that will probably not give Berlin a locational advantage in the next four years.
 
(3) Gothenburg, Monday. Urban Ahlin, Sweden’s former ambassador to the United States, on what the dependency costs when it is called in.
 
“For me it has been pain, physical pain, to see when Starlink has been taken down or totally blacked out, and the Ukrainian soldiers have simply died because someone has decided that you are no longer going to have that information.”
 
He is not arguing for autarky. He wants Sweden further inside the American technology ecosystem, not outside it. His word for what is missing is rådighet: control over what you can use, when you need it, without having to own it.
 
Ballheimer’s fax is what it looks like when the rådighet runs out.
 
Now the ask. The money is announced, the strategy is adopted, the architecture is proposed. What is missing is a signature.
 
So, to the defence ministry: name the date of the first German space programme awarded in lots.
 
Not the quarter. The date.
 
Next Wednesday I am delighted to moderate the 4th Commercial Space Law Workshop at Space Tech Expo in Bremen, with Ingo BAUMANN and Prof. Dr. Lesley Jane Smith: insurance, cybersecurity, orbital data centres. The unglamorous machinery, for a whole morning.

Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp has come out. He’s a progressive Democrat. I don’t care about his politics, but let’s look at his company and how inspiring he is for the next generation of entrepreneurs. 

Just one week after Democrats won control of both the US House and Senate, Karp has suddenly rediscovered his progressive politics.

In an interview with POLITICO he declared that he’s been a Democrat for his entire life, described himself as progressive 8 times, said Trump had gone too far on immigration, and said Democrats had done enough to potentially win his support in 2028.

“I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir - all of our products are essentially progressive”.

He now wants to talk about economic justice, saying that Democrats understand something Republicans don’t, which is that capitalism can’t solve every problem.

Let’s look at what Karp and Palantir have actually been doing while Trump has been in office.

In 2025, Trump’s United States Customs and Immigration Service awarded Palantir about $60M to build ImmigrationOS, tech that identifies people for deportation, prioritises arrests, tracks visa overstays and monitors voluntary departures from the US.

Palantir previously claimed it wouldn’t provide technology for broad immigration tracking, but expanded those operations under Trump. Karp defended Trump’s immigration policies in December 2025. He said extreme scepticism was the genuinely progressive position because immigration had depressed working class wages and caused social disruption in Europe.

He also described Palantir as “completely anti-woke” and criticised Democrats as “totally irresponsible”.

Karp donated to MAGA Inc. and Trump’s White House ballroom project, while Palantir executive Shyam Sankar was linked to a separate $10M ballroom contribution.

In July 2025, Palantir secured a US Army agreement worth up to $10B over 10 years, while the Pentagon allocated up to another $795M to its Maven military intelligence and targeting tech.

In 2024, Palantir partnered with Israel’s Ministry of Defence to provide technology to support its military operations during the war.

Following the Democrats’ election victory, Karp is now criticising Trump’s immigration policies and championing economic justice, claiming he’d privately expressed concerns about immigration enforcement all along.

But Palantir’s contracts, its products and Karp’s public statements tell a different story about what he was prepared to support while Trump controlled Washington.

Democrats will soon have the authority to investigate what Palantir provided to the Trump administration, how its technology was used, and if those activities complied with the law.

Now that Democrats control Congress, Karp is suddenly talking about economic justice and criticising Trump. But Palantir made billions from the same administration he’s now distancing himself from.

posts.title: If an AI tool's score matches your rejection, Colorado's draft rules presume the tool made the call.
posts.author: Alex Staff Agency
posts.snippet:
If an AI tool's score matches your rejection, Colorado's draft rules presume the tool made the call.

Colorado's draft rules for automated hiring decisions (4 CCR 904-6) are expected to apply from 1 January 2027. In Jackson Lewis' reading, a decision that matches the tool's output is presumed to have been "materially influenced" by it. A rubber-stamp review stops being a defence.

What the draft asks for: a plain-language notice that a tool is in use; reviewers who are trained, can override the result and look at the underlying evidence; a written explanation within 30 days; compliance records kept for at least three years. And on outside help: "you are responsible for compliance", even if a staffing firm assists.

This is not a Colorado-only story. Northeastern's survey of 8,174 hiring decision-makers found AI reads résumés first for 54% of them, and for 83% in tech. Few teams could show today who overrode a score last quarter, and why.

Caveats: this is a draft, we worked from law-firm summaries rather than the text itself, and it is not legal advice.

Start with a simple log: for each AI-ranked shortlist, who looked at it and what they changed. If a recruiting partner supplies the shortlist, the draft suggests the accountability still sits with you.

Could you show, for your last five rejections, who reviewed the AI's score and what they decided?
